newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Aznar, Gonzalez meet as feud clouds issues.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Aznar, Gonzalez meet as feud clouds issues.

text.p: Spain's Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar was meeting his predecessor and current opposition Socialist party leader Felipe Gonzalez on Thursday as a bitter war of words that has soured the political climate overshadowed other issues.

Ostensibly, the two are to use their first meeting in six months to trade views on the European Union and NATO ahead of upcoming summits, but there was speculation in political circles about whether they could put aside their differences.
"I hope both leaders agree that instead of insulting each other, they will talk about alternative proposals," said Julio Anguita, leader of the United Left, Spain's third largest political party.

Socialist party spokesman Cipria Ciscar said Gonzalez was prepared to talk about the bigger issues facing Spain but he worried that Aznar's one-year-old Popular Party government would not be able to rise above the political carping.

"Gonzalez is approaching (the meeting) with a good disposition but it is this government that has slandered, lied and defamed," he told journalists. "The current government threatens its adversary by interfering, making anonymous denouncements and acting in an undignified way for a democracy."

Squabbling between the Popular Party and the Socialists turned nasty last month when Gonzalez, speaking in Mexico, accused the deputy prime minister of conspiring to frame him for a 1980s "dirty war" against Basque separatists.

He also said the government had threatened to send a television executive to jail over disputed rights to view soccer matches. The executive, Antena 3 chairman Antonio Asensio, confirmed before Congress that he had received a threatening phone call from government spokesman Miguel Angel Rodriguez.
Rodriguez denies the allegation and has volunteered to answer questions in Congress on the issue.
Meanwhile, Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato has accused the former Socialist administration of giving a tax amnesty to its top officials by cooking accounts and even destroying documents.

The tit-for-tat accusations reached crisis level on Tuesday when the government's key parliamentary allies warned that they too were worried about the pressure Rodriguez had allegedly used with Asensio and that their support was far from guaranteed.
Foreign observers said the troubled atmosphere reflected the inexperience and immaturity of Aznar's cabinet, more than any real crisis.

"If anything, it shows Spain's democracy is still in its adolescence, if not its infancy," said one political expert. "I don't expect the house is about to fall. The Socialists survived much worse and then, as now, the feeling of insecurity centres on the prime minister's judgement in picking his people."
A foreign economist based in Madrid also dismissed the controversy as hot air, saying that it was not surprising that Rato had found accounting discrepancies.
"The essential thing about Spain's national accounting is that it's not supposed to be understood," the economist said.

Deputy Prime Minister Alvarez Cascos, who had vigorously fended off Gonzalez's conspiracy theories last month, on Thursday tried to play down the importance of the difficulties between the two top parties.

"It doesn't have to be dramatised. One just has to look at how the parliaments in Britian and France debate to see that we are exaggerating what is normal dialectic tension in democratic chambers," he told journalists.
But Spanish media expected the encounter to be tense with radio and television broadcasts saying political feuding would dominate over other issues.
